items.title: Sudan: Transfer War Crimes Suspects to ICC
items.description: Click to expand Image Left to right: Governor of South Kordofan Ahmed Haroun in South Kordofan State, August 23, 2011. © 2011 Reuters; Abdel Rahim Mohammed Hussein. © 2010 غيداء نجم الدين سعيد ابراهيم/Wikipedia; and Omar al-Bashir. © 2009 U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jesse B. Awalt/Wikipedia (The Hague) – Sudanese authorities should immediately transfer former Interior Minister Ahmed Haroun to the International Criminal Court (ICC) to face charges in The Hague, Human Rights Watch said today. Haroun was recently taken into Sudanese custody and faces ICC war crimes and crimes against humanity charges, committed in Sudan’s Darfur region, in 2003 and 2004. On November 8, 2026, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) reportedly re-arrested Haroun, interior minister of Sudan in 2007, when an ICC arrest warrant was issued against him. He was arrested one day after he took part in a video podcast interview, his first public appearance since 2019. The armed forces have not officially confirmed Haroun’s whereabouts, but media reported that he is detained in Khartoum state. “For two decades, victims of atrocity crimes in Darfur have witnessed Haroun and others evading justice, leading to impunity-fueled cycles of violence that are claiming more victims every day.” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “If Sudan’s authorities transferred those sought by the ICC to the court in The Hague, as they are obliged to do, it would send a powerful message to those committing crimes today that they too may find themselves in the dock.” Authorities should also transfer former President Omar al-Bashir—who is believed to be in Sudanese custody in Khartoum state as well—and locate, arrest, and transfer former Defense Minister Abdelrahim M. Hussein. The ICC has also issued arrest warrants for both of them, though there is no information available on Hussein’s location. The ICC issued an arrest warrant against Haroun in 2007, and another against Hussein in 2012, for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2004. During that period, Sudanese government forces and allied militias carried out targeted attacks against civilians on the basis of their ethnicity, including killings, rape, forced displacement from their homes and land, and burning of their villages. In 2009 and 2010, the ICC issued two arrest warrants against al-Bashir for alleged war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide committed in Darfur between 2003 and 2008. Following al-Bashir’s ouster in April 2019, Sudanese authorities held Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein in custody for charges not related to atrocities in Darfur but failed to transfer them to the ICC. After fighting erupted between SAF and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the authorities moved al-Bashir to Alia military hospital in Omdurman, Khartoum state, where he reportedly remained under guard, while Haroun left detention amid the collapse of prison security, and under circumstances suggesting coordination with judicial authorities. On September 30, 2026, SAF granted al-Bashir initial approval to travel outside of Sudan for medical treatment. Based on media reports, al-Bashir continues to receive medical care at Alia military hospital and is yet to travel abroad. UN Security Council Resolution 1593, referring the situation in Darfur to the ICC prosecutor, requires the government of Sudan to cooperate with the court even though it is not a party to the Rome Statute, the ICC’s founding treaty. In 2021, the ICC’s Office of the Prosecutor signed a memorandum of understanding with the Sudanese authorities addressing cooperation for arrests. The ICC lacks the ability to enforce its own orders and relies on state cooperation to conduct investigations and make arrests. In January and July, the Office of the Prosecutor reported to the United Nations Security Council on its investigation in Darfur, including its continued engagement with Sudanese authorities. In addition to addressing crimes from July 2002 onward, the Office of the Prosecutor is also investigating crimes committed since April 2023 in Darfur. The prosecutor’s office reported “positive” and “significant” cooperation by Sudanese authorities, and assistance in support of its investigative activities, including deployment of the office’s investigative team to Port Sudan. Nevertheless, Sudan has not fulfilled its obligation to carry out the court’s arrest warrants and transfer the wanted suspects to the Hague. The authorities should provide public information on the whereabouts of all the wanted suspects and take immediate steps to allow their transfer to the court, Human Rights Watch said. The African Union, the members of the Atrocity Prevention and Justice Coalition for Sudan–– particularly the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Sierra Leone––as well as the European Union and its member states should directly engage with Sudanese authorities, calling on them to comply with their obligation to fully cooperate with the ICC and to transfer Haroun, al-Bashir, and Hussein to the court’s custody. ICC judges have referred to the Security Council several findings of noncooperation against Sudan and ICC member states in relation to the arrest of ICC suspects. However, the council has never taken steps to enforce these findings. UN member states should urge the Security Council to back the ICC’s mandate in Darfur, including by enforcing the court’s findings of noncooperation on arrests. The ICC prosecutor’s office should use its next biannual report to the council, in January 2027, as an opportunity to raise any concerns related to Sudan’s cooperation on arrests. In 2025, the ICC convicted Ali Muhammad Ali Abd-Al-Rahman (also known as Ali Kosheib), a former leader of Sudan’s “Janjaweed” militias, for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur in 2003 and 2004, and sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Kosheib’s trial was possible after he surrendered himself voluntarily to the ICC’s custody in 2020. “For victims and survivors of crimes in Darfur, Sudanese authorities’ promises of cooperation mean little without concrete action,” Evenson said. “Sudan’s international partners should use every diplomatic tool at their disposal to press for the immediate transfer of all ICC suspects in Sudanese custody and make clear that cooperation with the court is not optional.”

Gun can kill terrorists, only education can kill terrorism – Buratai
items.description: The former Chief of Army Staff, retired Lt.-Gen. Tukur Buratai has called for inclusive education and wider access to learning opportunities, saying they are critical to addressing the conditions that sustain terrorism and violent extremism in Nigeria. Buratai made the call at the 2026 Young Adult Literature Prize Award and unveiling of the 2025 anthology of the T.Y. Buratai Literary Initiative (TYBLI), on Wednesday in Nasarawa State. The former Nigerian Ambassador to Benin Republic said military force alone could not defeat terrorism without deliberate investment in education, intellectual development and the minds of young Nigerians. “Gun can kill a terrorist, but only education can kill terrorism,” he declared. Buratai said national development must go beyond infrastructure, military strength and economic resources to include the intellectual capacity, creative imagination and moral consciousness of citizens. He stressed that young Nigerians, irrespective of their backgrounds, needed equal opportunities, platforms and encouragement to develop their talents and contribute meaningfully to society. The former COAS said the initiative was established on the conviction that great nations were built not only by strong armies and economies but also by ideas, literature and educated citizens. He urged universities to promote young adult literature through research, teaching and programmes that encouraged creativity, critical thinking and intellectual development. “A school that produces excellent academic results but neglects imagination and critical thinking has not fully prepared its students for the future,” he said. Buratai said the initiative had, since 2023, provided a platform for young Nigerians from diverse backgrounds to demonstrate their creativity and move from passive consumption to active production of literature. He described the unveiling of the 2025 anthology as another milestone, providing a permanent record of the imagination, creativity and achievements of young authors. He also announced plans to introduce full scholarships for deserving winners within the next three to five years, to enable them to complete their education. In a goodwill message, the Vice-Chancellor of Nasarawa State University, Keffi, Prof. Sa’adatu Liman, described young adult literature as an important bridge between childhood and adulthood. Liman said literature helped young people confront questions of identity, courage, faith, justice and leadership through stories that reflected their experiences. She described the initiative as an investment in human development and nation-building, pledging the university’s readiness to strengthen its partnership with TYBLI. Also, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Ibadan, Prof. Peter Olamakinde Olapegba, commended the initiative for recognising the importance of academic leadership, scholarship and research mentorship. Olapegba, who received an award for excellence in academic leadership and research mentorship, said the recognition affirmed the importance of building capacity and nurturing future generations. He dedicated the award to his colleagues, mentors, students and mentees, particularly five PhD students who graduated from the university on the eve of the event. “The true reward of mentorship is not simply what we accomplish as individuals, but the lives we influence, the capacity we build and the legacy we leave behind,” he said. Olapegba said the award had renewed his commitment to scholarship, service and the development of future generations. The event featured the presentation of awards to outstanding young writers and the unveiling of the 2025 anthology. (NAN) The post Gun can kill terrorists, only education can kill terrorism – Buratai appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: We’re negotiating livelihoods, not climate – Africa presses for climate finance at COP31
items.description: For millions of Africans facing increasingly unpredictable rainfall, prolonged droughts, devastating floods and other extreme weather events, the outcome of climate negotiations is more than a diplomatic agreement. It is a question of survival, livelihoods and economic security. From farming communities struggling with changing rainfall patterns to households displaced by floods and coastal communities threatened by rising sea levels, the consequences of climate change are increasingly being felt across the continent. Yet, as world leaders and negotiators gather in Antalya, Türkiye, for the second week of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), African representatives say the continent’s ability to respond to these impacts will depend largely on whether developed countries deliver the financial commitments needed to support climate action. The Chair of the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), Nana Dr. Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, made this point during an engagement with African civil society organisations, where he briefed them on the state of negotiations and the continent’s priorities for the remainder of the conference. He acknowledged growing concerns about extreme weather events, including El Niño-related climate disruptions, but noted that such realities often find expression in negotiations only through technical discussions and references in negotiated texts. He said several international funding mechanisms, including the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, the Adaptation Fund and the Green Climate Fund, have been established to support developing countries in addressing climate impacts. However, Africa needs more resources flowing into these mechanisms to enable vulnerable countries to access the support required to respond to climate-related disasters. “That is why the negotiators are fighting for more money into these funds for developing countries to capitalise on these funds to address some of these disasters,” he said. Dr. Amoah said the AGN had arrived at COP31 with considerable ambition to advance implementation of the Paris Agreement, but stressed that such ambition must be matched with the necessary financial and technical support. The group’s priorities include strengthening ambition towards the global temperature goal, building climate resilience and securing the means of implementation. “For us at AGN, implementation needs means of implementation,” he stressed. Climate finance remains a major sticking point Providing an update on the state of negotiations, Dr. Amoah identified climate finance, the progression of adaptation finance and a more comprehensive approach to just transition as key areas of focus for the African negotiating bloc. He admitted that negotiations on climate finance had been among the most difficult, particularly efforts to advance discussions on the obligations of developed countries under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement. The provision addresses the responsibility of developed countries to provide financial resources to assist developing countries with climate mitigation and adaptation. “Our interest is to advance the conversation of Article 9.1, which talks about the provision of climate finance, and that’s the reason why we are pushing for the adoption of the work programme as part of the agenda,” he said. He argued that the financial requirements of developing countries were enormous, considering the climate commitments outlined in their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), National Adaptation Plans and other national development frameworks. African economies, he noted, were already vulnerable to climate impacts, with governments having to contend with the mounting economic costs of disasters and the resources required to build resilience. The AGN Chair expressed concern about what he described as attempts by developed countries to shift attention away from their responsibilities on emissions reduction and climate finance towards broader global targets. On just transition, he said Africa was seeking an outcome that addresses the continent’s development priorities and recognises the support required to transition towards sustainable and climate-resilient economies. However, he raised concerns that the negotiating text did not adequately reflect the means of implementation needed to deliver such a transition. “It is a difficult situation now. We either get a good outcome or don’t get any outcome because a bad outcome is dangerous,” he cautioned. ‘We are negotiating livelihoods, not climate’ For African civil society organisations, the stakes extend beyond the technical language of the negotiating texts. Executive Director of the Pan-African Climate Justice Alliance (PACJA), Dr. Mithika Mwenda, said African civil society groups were looking to the AGN to secure an outcome that responds to the continent’s development and climate justice concerns. He emphasised that the negotiations must be understood in the context of the lives and economic aspirations of ordinary Africans. “We’re not negotiating climate; we are negotiating livelihoods, we are negotiating our economies, we are negotiating our development,” Dr. Mwenda said. His remarks reflect growing concerns among African civil society groups that the failure to secure adequate climate finance could undermine efforts to protect vulnerable communities, strengthen food systems and support sustainable development. Ghana’s Minister of Environment, Science and Technology, Dr. Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, also underscored the human cost of unfulfilled climate finance commitments. She said Africa contributes relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions but continues to suffer disproportionately from the consequences of climate change. “The important thing is for the world to understand that Africa appreciates the fact that it does not contribute significantly to the climate crisis; it’s suffering the most, and every time that the promises that are made in terms of the delivery on finance are not fulfilled, these are lives lost, these are livelihoods destroyed… everything is at risk,” she said. The Minister urged African negotiators to remain firm in advancing the continent’s interests and to draw attention to parties whose positions, in her view, obstruct progress on agreed commitments. She said the outcome of COP31 would be important in laying the groundwork for the next climate conference, COP32. “We are looking forward to a great, successful COP32, but that can only be if we plant the right seeds here at COP31. We must not let it be said that the COP32 was not able to achieve much,” she said. As negotiations enter their decisive phase in Antalya, African countries are pushing for commitments that translate into accessible financing, stronger adaptation support and a just transition that reflects their development realities. For communities already bearing the cost of climate change, however, the measure of success will ultimately be whether the promises made in international negotiating rooms translate into resources, protection and opportunities on the ground.

items.title: FAAC shares N2.4trn among FG, states, LGs in October
items.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) has shared the sum of N2.441 trillion among the three tiers of government. The amount was from the October 2026 Federation Account Revenue, which was shared at the FAAC meeting held in Abuja on Wednesday. The N2.441 trillion comprised distributable statutory revenue of N1.688 trillion and Value Added Tax (VAT) revenue of N752.488 billion. A communiqué issued by the Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) indicated that gross revenue of N3.811 trillion was available in the month of October 2026. Total deduction for cost of collection was N128.797 billion while total transfers, refunds and savings stood at N1.241 trillion. According to the communiqué sent to media houses by Bawa Mokwa, Director of Press of the Office of the Accountant-General of the Federation, Wednesday night, gross statutory revenue of N2.999 trillion was received for the month of October 2026. This was lower than the sum of N3.096 trillion received in the preceding month by N97.323 billion. Gross revenue of N812.446 billion was available from the Value Added Tax (VAT) in October 2026. This was lower than the N816.872 billion available in the month of September 2026 by N4.426 billion. The communiqué stated that from the N2.441 trillion total distributable revenue, the Federal Government received a total sum of N856.065 billion and the state governments received a total sum of N809.909 billion. The Local Government Councils received N568.701 billion, while the sum of N206.384 billion (13% of mineral revenue) was shared to the benefiting State as derivation revenue. On the N1.688 trillion distributable statutory revenue, the Federal Government received N780.816 billion and the State Governments received N396.040 billion. The Local Government Councils received N305.331 billion and the sum of N206.384 billion (13% of mineral revenue) was shared to the benefiting States as derivation revenue. From the N752.488 billion distributable Value Added Tax (VAT) revenue, the Federal Government received N75.249 billion, the State Governments received N413.868 billion and the Local Government Councils received N263.371 billion. In October 2026, Excise Duty and CET Levies increased marginally, while Petroleum Profit Tax (PPT), Hydrocarbon Tax (HT), Petroleum Royalties, Import Duty, Companies Income Tax (CIT), CGT & SDT, Value Added Tax (VTA), Mineral Royalties, and Gas Flared Penalty, Rental Gas Flared Fee and Misc. Oil Revenue all decreased. The post FAAC shares N2.4trn among FG, states, LGs in October appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: UGEL CEO defends hostel rent increase, cites rising utility costs, inflation and exchange rates
items.description: The Chief Executive Officer of the University of Ghana Enterprises Limited (UGEL), Yawo Nutifafa Agbesi, has defended the increase in hostel fees, citing rising utility costs, exchange rate fluctuations and inflation as some of the factors putting pressure on the company’s operations. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Wednesday, November 18, he said these factors had affected the company’s day-to-day running costs over the past three years, necessitating adjustments to its charges. He acknowledged that inflation and the exchange rate had been relatively stable in 2026 but said UGEL had still faced additional costs following changes to the Value Added Tax (VAT) regime. “Even for 2026, where the inflation rate has been very stable for this year and the exchange rate has been really good, we had to encounter a 4%… You know, the VAT moved from 4% flat VAT to 20%. So if we were buying, for example, an item which was a thousand cedis, and then the VAT moves from 4% to 20%, it just throws our budget totally out of control,” he said. Mr Agbesi also acknowledged that UGEL owed a consortium of banks about GH¢70 million and was expected to repay GH¢38 million this year. However, he rejected the suggestion that students were being made to bear the cost of the company’s borrowing decisions, explaining that the loan was only one of several factors affecting its operations. “I’m not saying that because we have a loan to pay, we are passing on the full cost of the loan to the student. The loan is one of the variables that also affect our business,” he said. He maintained that the company was not increasing hostel fees indiscriminately, despite the rising costs. According to him, the various factors had increased UGEL’s operational costs by an estimated 30 to 40 per cent, but the company had moderated its adjustments in recognition of the financial circumstances of students and their families. “Despite these variables, which averagely affect our business in terms of cost by about 30 to 40 per cent, our increments have always been that we take into consideration the fact that the average Ghanaian is entitled to education,” he added.

Tinubu hails Alake of Egbaland’s 21-year reign
items.description: ‎‎By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ‎ ‎President Bola Tinubu has paid tribute to the Alake of Egbaland, Oba Adedotun Aremu Gbadebo III, describing his 21 years on the throne as a testament to selfless service and dedication to his people’s welfare. ‎ ‎The President in a tribute marking the monarch’s anniversary, praised his commitment to development, cultural preservation and responsible leadership. ‎ ‎“Your Majesty, 21 years on the throne is no ordinary milestone. It is a remarkable testament to your selfless service and dedication to your people’s welfare,” the President said. ‎ ‎Tinubu saluted the monarch’s military career before his ascension, highlighting the principles that defined his service to the nation. ‎ ‎“Your Majesty, your journey to the revered throne was preceded by your distinguished and illustrious military career, where discipline, courage, patriotism, loyalty, and a deep sense of duty formed the core of your guiding principles in serving the nation.” ‎ ‎The President said the Alake’s reign had witnessed development within the Egba kingdom and across the state, underscoring the contribution of traditional institutions to governance and development. ‎ ‎“For 21 remarkable years, your reign has witnessed tremendous development, not only within the Egba kingdom but also across the state. ‎ ‎”These strides in development stand as enduring reminders of the invaluable role of the traditional institution in complementing governments of the day for overall development.” ‎ ‎Tinubu also commended the monarch’s dedication to preserving cultural heritage and acknowledged the influence of his counsel on elected leaders. ‎ ‎“Your unwavering commitment to preserving and promoting our rich cultural heritage deserves commendation and emulation across all strata,” he said. ‎ ‎“Your words of advice, with consistent emphasis on responsible leadership, humility, accountability, service to the people, and respect for institutions, continue to guide us as elected leaders of the people.” ‎ ‎Congratulating the sons and daughters of Egbaland, the President said God had answered their prayers for a king distinguished by wisdom, humility and dedication to service. ‎ ‎“As you celebrate this remarkable anniversary, I congratulate the sons and daughters of Egbaland that Almighty God answered their prayers for a King filled with wisdom, dedication to service, humility and whose reign will be known for peace and development.” ‎ ‎The President concluded his tribute with prayer, saying: “May Almighty God grant Your Majesty sound health, renewed strength, divine wisdom and many more fruitful and peaceful years on the throne.” The post Tinubu hails Alake of Egbaland’s 21-year reign appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: « La Francophonie se situe au carrefour de son existence »
items.description: Avec plus de 50 années d’existence et plus de 390 millions de locuteurs, la Francophonie doit s’adapter aux défis et enjeux du monde contemporain, d’après professeur Oumar Ba. Docteur en droit et en science politique, enseignant au Centre d’Études Diplomatiques et Stratégiques (Ceds) de Paris, et aussi professeur invité à l'Université Senghor de la Francophonie, Oumar Ba estime que cette organisation est au carrefour de son existence. Les tensions sur le choix du Secrétairegénéral de l’Organisation internationale de la Francophonie lors du XXe Sommet des Chefs d’État et Chefs de gouvernement ont mis en lumière cette institution vieille de 56 ans. Créée en 1970 au Niger, l’Oif a connu du chemin et des mutations. Selon, Oumar Ba, professeur invité à l'Université Senghor de la Francophonie, cette organisation doit faire sa mue et s’adapter au contexte actuel. « La Francophonie se situe au carrefour de son existence. Elle devra faire sa mue en s'adaptant et en se réinventant en permanence ; sinon, elle sera dépassée par les défis et enjeux contemporains », a affirmé Oumar Ba, dans un entretien avec Le Soleil. Docteur en droit et en science politique, Oumar Ba est aussi enseignant au Centre d’Études Diplomatiques et Stratégiques (Ceds) de Paris. D’après lui, la Francophonie compte 396 millions de locuteurs, dont 65 % vivent en Afrique et la moitié a moins de 30 ans. « Elle polarise 90 États et gouvernements et 170 millions d'apprenants du et en français. Ce qui en fait la 4e langue parlée du monde et aussi sur le Net. La jeunesse de cet espace géopolitique constitue un atout important pour l'organisation en termes de potentiel de marché sur le plan géoéconomique, mais il n'est pas encore très intégré au niveau structurel », a-t-il souligné. M. Ba a ajouté que la dimension géopolitique de la Francophonie, en tant que cadre systémique diplomatique international très vaste, en fait un puissant levier d'influence diplomatique ou de diplomatie d'influence en termes de « soft power » (pouvoir de persuasion) pour les États du continent africain. « Elle est aussi une organisation de pourparlers pour la gestion, la médiation, les bons offices et la résolution pacifique des différends entre ses membres. Elle sert également de vecteur de formation et de mise à niveau des diplomates et des étudiants via des programmes comme la classe diplomatique, les séminaires diplomatiques, les bourses francophones et l’Association des universités partiellement ou entièrement de langue française (Aupelf), l’Agence universitaire de la Francophonie(Auf) entre autres », a poursuivi M. Ba. D’après lui, les réseaux des organisations de la société civile, des médias, des journalistes voire des jeunes renforcent l’intérêt stratégique de la Francophonie pour l'Afrique. « Ce perfectionnement dans les sciences et les échanges de bonnes pratiques entre eux, ainsi que les activités artistiques francophones, constituent des facteurs de découverte des talents du continent et de dialogue des cultures. Ce qui constitue le socle de sa diplomatie culturelle porteuse de dividendes », a justifié Oumar Ba. Sur le plan de l'appui technique à la consolidation démocratique et de l'État de droit, M. Ba a cité le soutien apporté par la Francophonie aux pays africains pour les aider à faire des réformes consensuelles, inclusives et consolidantes, favorisant la plupart du temps le retour ordonné à l'ordre constitutionnel, la transparence des processus électoraux et l'alternance au pouvoir. « La Francophonie le fait souvent en étroite coordination avec l'Union africaine et les communautés économiques régionales impliquées, les autres partenaires techniques et financiers et les sociétés civiles nationales. Ses missions d'assistance électorale sont importantes et ont permis à des États de régler des crises profondes autour de la fiabilité du fichier électoral », a-t-il précisé. Malgré cela, a indiqué M. Ba, les pays africains francophones souhaitent voir la Francophonie contribuer plus fortement à les appuyer dans leur quête de maîtrise de l'IA et de transfert technologique nécessaire à impulser leur développement. « Ils veulent qu'elle soutienne plus énergiquement leurs revendications en faveur de la réforme globale du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies et de l'architecture économique et financière internationale où l'Afrique sera présente avec plus de poids pour contribuer à la prise de décisions par elle-même, sans aucun intermédiaire », a mentionné Oumar Ba. items.title: Election Denialism Is All but Dead
items.description: O ut of all the surprises of the 2026 midterm election, among the most heartening was Donald Trump’s willingness to accept the results. “We’ll probably work something out,” he told The New York Times of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress. The next day, he walked the press around the site of the planned White House ballroom, less interested in battling over the election than showing off his construction project. This newfound tranquility did not last: In the weeks since the midterms, Trump has begun sharing posts on his Truth Social feed casting doubt on the integrity of the vote. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” he asked on November 9. But a few stray posts on a bespoke social-media site are trifling compared with the aggressive campaign of propaganda, litigation, and brute force that Trump used to attempt to subvert the 2020 presidential vote. Six years after Trump launched the election-denialist movement, the Big Lie of election fraud might finally be ebbing as a defining force in American politics. K ate Starbird, a University of Washington professor, monitored online election rumors in 2020 as they gained momentum. She has described the growth of election denialism that year as a dynamic of “participatory propaganda”—a feedback loop between political elites such as Trump, who seeded ideas about voter fraud, and the many Americans who responded to those suggestions by seeking out further evidence of supposed trickery. Through this process, what started with claims by Trump in the spring of 2020 about the supposed unreliability of mail-in ballots escalated into the attack on the Capitol on January 6. In the following years, election deniers continued to build their movement, taking positions as state and local election administrators and preparing to subvert—or, depending on your point of view, protect—the vote. When Trump took power again in 2025, election denialism essentially became the official policy of the United States government. The FBI seized ballots from 2020 in Georgia’s Fulton County; the Justice Department demanded voter records from every state in the union, fueling theories that the voter rolls were riddled with inaccuracies; and, as the midterms grew closer, federal authorities grew more and more aggressive in seeking to shape the election in the GOP’s favor. Experts, election officials, and civil-society groups were wary that grassroots election deniers, together with the White House, might seek to upend either the voting process or the counting of ballots. [ Read: The election deniers are in retreat ] Yet many Republican candidates who had previously complained about rigged elections stayed quiet on the subject, perhaps worried that emphasizing claims of election fraud could push their supporters to stay home rather than vote. And as the magnitude of the Republican loss on Election Day became clear, election deniers remained similarly docile. Scott Perry, a Republican representative from Pennsylvania who drew the attention of federal prosecutors for his close involvement in the effort to overturn the 2020 election, conceded promptly to his Democratic challenger in remarks that emphasized the importance of “the peaceful transfer of authority that is paramount to our Republic.” Ali Alexander, a far-right activist and founder of the group Stop the Steal, which helped organize the rally at the Ellipse on January 6, 2021, released a statement on Telegram that “STOP THE STEAL SAYS MIDTERM WIPEOUT ELECTION WAS LEGITIMATE” and “WILL NOT PROTEST.” As Election Day unfolded, Starbird told me, her team at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public found that rumors of fraud didn’t gain the same traction as in 2020. When polls opened that morning, election workers in Westchester County, New York, discovered that voting machines were not properly scanning ballots—a logistical hiccup that generated conspiratorial online posts on both the left and right. The incident was similar to glitches in Arizona’s Maricopa County during the 2022 midterms, which grew into viral rumors of election fraud and became the focus of long-running complaints by Kari Lake, the GOP candidate who lost the Arizona governor’s race that year. Comparing posts on Twitter (now X) from both incidents, Starbird’s team found that “the overall content and attention around the events in Westchester was about 20 percent on Election Day as the attention around Maricopa,” Starbird said. In the days immediately after the vote, they continued to see only “very low” activity concerning election denial online. At first, that quiet might have been attributable to Trump’s own apparent lack of interest in such conspiracies. Midterms typically occasion less public attention than presidential elections, and perhaps that was personally true for the president—who, unlike in 2020, was not on the ballot. In the absence of angry posts from the president, election deniers had little to coalesce around. Online interest in conspiracy theories increased once Trump started to dabble in his old fraud claims, Starbird told me, though still nowhere close to where it was in 2020. “They just don’t have all the ingredients they would need for a large-scale attempt to try to subvert election results,” she said. The results themselves were arguably the biggest problem for any such attempt. The midterms were not just a Democratic victory but a total blowout—the biggest margin of House victory in a midterm for any party since the post-Watergate election of 1974. The resounding rejection of GOP governance left Republicans dejected, too stunned to attempt any unified subversion of the results. Major right-wing outlets such as Fox and Newsmax, which pushed election denial aggressively in 2020, did not attempt to rally the troops after 2026. “We’re seeing a few more activist journalists, people that work for hyperpartisan outlets, begin to play with this,” Starbird told me, but not “more mainstream conservative political voices.” After Trump shared speculation about rigged voting machines on Truth Social, the former Fox host Megyn Kelly posted on X, “Just stop.” Republican politicians, meanwhile, appear to have largely moved on to intraparty bickering. [ Jonathan Chait: The Left’s election denial ] MAGA may have been cannibalized in part by its own success. In 2020, Starbird has argued, the Big Lie thrived on the participation of true believers. In 2026, with the federal government itself promoting election denialism, those supporters were less inclined to take action themselves. “They were waiting for the Trump administration” to sweep in and seize ballots or otherwise save the day, Starbird told me. When Trump didn’t—because he had no power to do so—the grassroots was no longer primed to take action. On X, posts from right-wing influencers toying with the notion of a stolen election have accreted bitter comments. “Nothing will be done. It’s all a big dog and pony show. Sick of it,” complained the prominent Trump supporter @catturd2 in a Friday post, responding to a post from GOP Senator Ron Johnson casting doubt on election results in the Alaska Senate race. Perhaps conspiracy theories of election fraud have just gotten old. Like a network television show renewed one too many times, the characters are stale, the plots familiar, the twists lacking surprise. When the election-denial movement first took off in the spring and summer of 2020, it was responding to circumstances that were genuinely novel—a global pandemic that necessitated a rapid shift toward mail-in balloting—and drawing on the crackling right-wing political energy of anti-mask and -lockdown protests. Six years later, that energy has dissipated. Trump himself is no longer a crusading outsider but a symbol of the stagnant political establishment that, a decade ago, he promised to upend. Election officials have worked hard to allay public fears about the integrity of the electoral process. People have different things on their minds, such as inflation and high gas prices caused by Trump’s war of choice in Iran. A half-decade-old story about Democrats stealing elections doesn’t speak to those concerns. “The kind of widespread election denialism that undermines trust in democracy, that could be used and weaponized to contest election results—I’m hopeful that that is not as much of a threat going forward,” Starbird told me. Still, she emphasized that election lies are not entirely gone. “On the right, there is a deep story about how elections have been rigged against them in recent years,” she said. “And we may see another rigged-election narrative” arise in the future. What that narrative will be, though, remains undetermined. As Trump’s power wanes, the Republican Party and the American far right, newly freed from his orbit, will be forced to search for new causes to rally around. Election fraud may no longer be among them.

items.title: Galamsey fight: NAIMOS won’t sacrifice its mandate on the altar of political convenience – Spokesperson
items.description: The National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) has vowed to remain firm in its fight against illegal mining, insisting it will not compromise its mandate to accommodate political interests or convenience. The Secretariat’s Spokesperson, Paa Kwesi Schandorf said protecting Ghana’s environment should take precedence over political interests, arguing that the devastating effects of illegal mining do not discriminate between members of the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) and the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP). Mr Schandorf maintained that environmental protection must not be sacrificed on the altar of political convenience, stressing that the campaign against illegal mining requires a collective national commitment. “The fight against illegal mining should not be animated by politics. Indeed, the preservation of our environment should not be on the altar of political convenience,” he said. Speaking in an interview with Accra based TV3, the NAIMOS spokesperson said President John Dramani Mahama and the Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, had been unequivocal about the need to keep political considerations out of the anti-galamsey campaign. According to him, the government’s position has been clear, adding that there has not been any explicit political interference in the operations of the anti-illegal mining initiative over the period. He argued that the environmental consequences of illegal mining affect all citizens, irrespective of their political affiliations, making it inappropriate for the campaign to be driven by partisan interests. “When the waters are polluted, it doesn’t mind whether it is NDC members who are going to drink that water or NPP people who are going to drink that water,” he said. Mr Schandorf stressed that the indiscriminate nature of environmental destruction should inform the approach to tackling illegal mining, insisting that the campaign must remain focused on protecting the country’s natural resources. “So if the effect does not discriminate, then the fight cannot also be inspired by any political aspirations whatsoever,” he added. He maintained that the preservation of water bodies and other natural resources requires sustained commitment from all stakeholders, regardless of their political affiliations.

items.title: Air strikes kill 21 ISWAP terrorists in Borno
items.description: By Kingsley Omonobi In a significant operational success, precision air strikes conducted by the Air Assets of Joint Task Force (North East), Operation Hadin Kai (OPHK), between 16 and 17 November 2026, have neutralised 21 Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters and severely injured 10 others in separate operations around Monguno and the South Lake Chad area of Borno State. A statement signed by Captain Mohammed Goni, Acting Military Information Officer, said, “The first operation followed intelligence reports of ISWAP fighters advancing towards Monguno. “Acting on the intelligence, an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) established surveillance over the area and identified terrorists moving along a bush path northeast of Monguno. “The subsequent precision strike neutralised seven fighters, including members of the terrorist group’s Improvised Explosive Device (IED) network. Further confirmation revealed that Abba Bomma, identified as a key IED team expert, was incapacitated, while four other fighters sustained severe injuries. “In a separate operation at Arinna in the South Lake Chad area, precision air strikes dealt a significant blow to ISWAP’s leadership and operational structure. Among those neutralised was Malkam Sharki, a prominent member of the group’s Shura Council and Amirul Amniya (Provost Commander). “Also neutralised was ABU SAAD, the Qaid of Sabon Tumbu. Twelve additional fighters were eliminated, while five others sustained severe injuries. Several terrorist motorcycles were also destroyed during the operation. “Altogether, the two operations accounted for 21 ISWAP fighters neutralised and 10 severely injured. “The strikes have significantly degraded the group’s leadership structure, disrupted its IED network and weakened its operational capabilities. “The Theatre Command reaffirms its resolve to maintain sustained operational pressure on terrorists until lasting peace and normalcy are restored across the North East. “Residents are encouraged to continue supporting security agencies with credible and timely information.” The post Air strikes kill 21 ISWAP terrorists in Borno appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Relief for ASWAJ Islamic SHS as Techiman South MP donates 200 desks
items.description: The ASWAJ Islamic Senior High School in Techiman South has received a major boost to its infrastructure, with the delivery of 200 mono desks promised by the Member of Parliament, Martin Adjei Mensah Korsah. The desks, handed over on behalf of the MP by the former Municipal Chief Executive of Techiman, Hon. Benjamin Yaw Gyarko, are set to ease the school’s furniture challenges and enhance teaching and learning. The donation fulfills a promise made by the MP in October this year, when he paid a surprise visit to the school and witnessed firsthand the infrastructure strain caused by rapid enrollment growth. The brief handover ceremony was attended by constituency party executives, including the Constituency Chairman, as well as school officials, students, and parents. Speaking at the event, Mr Gyarko emphasized that the MP remains committed to supporting the school in diverse ways to improve its educational performance. “We are here today to fulfill the promise made by our MP,” he said. “He pledged 200 mono desks to support this school, and today, we are handing them over. The MP has assured that he will continue to support ASWAJ Islamic SHS in diverse ways to improve educational performance.” For the Headmaster of the school, Issah Sumaila Bahesi, the swift delivery of the desks is worthy of commendation. He noted that the donation will significantly mitigate the challenges the school was facing. “When the MP made the promise, we were hopeful. But to see the desks arrive within such a short period is truly commendable,” Mr. Bahesi said. “This will help address the sitting issues we were facing. We are grateful, and we pray for more support to tackle our other challenges, especially bunk beds for our boarding students.” The gesture has also brought joy to parents, who see it as a sign of the MP’s commitment to education in the constituency. Mama Shaban, a parent, shared her gratitude on behalf of other parents. “We are very thankful to the MP for this gesture. Our children now have proper desks to sit on,” she said. “We pray that he continues to support the school so our children can learn in a better environment.” The ASWAJ Islamic Senior High School, established in 2024, is the first and only public SHS in the Bono East Region. It opened with just 50 students but has since grown to nearly 600, with over 450 first-year students admitted this term alone. While the delivery of the 200 desks addresses one of the school’s most pressing needs, the institution still faces challenges, particularly regarding accommodation. The school is in dire need of bunk beds to accommodate its growing boarding population. The MP’s fulfilled promise has given the school community a reason to smile and hope for more support. With continued investment in infrastructure, the ASWAJ fraternity believes the school can live up to its potential as a center of academic excellence and moral discipline in the Bono East Region. For now, the students of ASWAJ Islamic SHS can sit comfortably at their new desks—a tangible reminder that promises made can indeed be kept.

items.title: Can Pope Leo Bridge the Church’s Demographic Divide?
items.description: Pope Leo XIV is leading the Catholic Church during a period of extraordinary demographic change. A century ago, Europeans dominated the Church, representing some two-thirds of the world’s Catholics. Today, Latin America and Africa together make up a majority. As a result of this shift, influence within the Church is quickly being redistributed from the West to the global South, two regions with often-competing ideas about the faith. As Leo emphasized on his landmark trip to South America this month, one of his principal goals is to keep the Church united. Maintaining unity has been a challenge for nearly every pontiff, but few of them have overseen a group of believers who are as far-flung and culturally diverse as the one he heads. Given his biography, Leo may be an ideal pope for the job. But he’ll have to bridge a set of divisions that are likely to intensify as the Church’s center of power continues to move. In many ways, the Church’s demographic transformation was personified by Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis. In 2013, Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Argentina became the first pontiff from the global South. As pope, he paid special attention to migration, poverty, and climate change, focusing on the disproportionate burdens these issues placed on the developing world. He also emerged as one of the most prominent critics of the West, condemning capitalist excess and even challenging NATO. [ Read: Why Pope Francis isn’t with the West on Ukraine ] Leo, too, has embodied the Church’s transition from the West toward the South. He’s the first pope born in the United States, but his formative pastoral experience came in Peru, where he served as a priest and bishop for 20 years and, in 2015, became a citizen. “That act symbolized a bond that this people had been weaving into my life long before,” he recalled during his visit to Lima this month. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you.” The pope’s connection to Latin America will be an important asset to him now that the region accounts for more than 40 percent of Catholics, twice Europe’s share. The global South’s growing representation has given it a stronger voice within the Church, and pastors there seem more and more unwilling to let Europe tell them what to do. Much of this resistance has come from Africa, the Church’s fastest-growing region, which Leo visited in April—the longest trip of his papacy until this month’s journey through South America. In recent years, African bishops have criticized the Church’s “Eurocentric” agenda, which they felt imposed an overly liberal approach on certain social issues. At a Vatican synod in 2014, one German cardinal complained that merely discussing homosexuality with his African peers was “taboo” and therefore impossible. “They should not tell us too much what we have to do,” the cardinal said, a remark that prompted the African leaders to organize a separate meeting and come up with a unified response. Two years later, many African bishops condemned Francis’s efforts to allow divorced and remarried Catholics to receive Communion in limited circumstances. In 2024, they refused to implement a declaration by Francis that authorized formal blessings of people in same-sex unions. During a synod held from 2021 to 2024, pastors from the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Oceania repeatedly condemned efforts by Western leaders in the Church to push “niche issues” such as women’s ordination as priests and the relaxation of Church teaching on homosexuality. As Leo told me last year in his first sit-down interview as pope, a cardinal from the Middle East approached him during the synod and lamented that pastors in the West are “obsessed with sexuality.” Like Francis, Leo has become one of the world’s leading advocates for the global South. In response to a question about migration during his return flight from Africa, he issued one of his most direct appeals on its behalf: “What is the global North doing to help the global South, or those countries where young people today cannot find a future and therefore dream of moving North?” the pope asked. Leo has also become one of the loudest voices challenging the West, drawing the ire of some of America’s most powerful men. In my interview with Leo, he expressed concern about Elon Musk becoming the world’s first trillionaire, which prompted Musk to respond on X with a quote from the Gospel of Matthew: “Why do you see the speck in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?” In September, the tech mogul Peter Thiel called the pope a “useful idiot” for the Chinese Communist Party because of his advocacy for stricter AI regulation. And most notable, President Trump lashed out at Leo in April when the pope condemned the Iran war. [ Peter Wehner: The American pope vs. the American president ] As part of his effort to restore U.S. dominance in Latin America, Trump has tried to curtail migration—another source of tension between the president and the pope. Thanks to the region’s swing to the right , Trump has found many leaders there who are sympathetic with him on the issue. Leo met with one of them this month in Argentina: President Javier Milei, who has courted Trump’s favor by offering his nation as a haven for data centers. Local Catholic leaders have criticized Milei, especially over his austere economic policies, which led some observers to expect that his meeting with Leo would be tense. But Milei became tearful as he said goodbye to the pope, a likely sign of how much influence Leo’s voice carries in the region, where he drew the largest crowds of any event he’s held, in Rome or abroad. Throughout his travels, Leo has appealed to the Catholic roots shared by both secular European societies, such as Spain and France, and Latin America, where the faith remains culturally prominent but Mass attendance is falling. Last week in Argentina, Leo pointed to that shared heritage as a means of “learning to live together, even amid differences of opinion.” This lingering cultural faith has been essential in Leo’s efforts to keep the Church united. But secularization is depleting its supply. As the Church’s demographics continue to change—and as its priorities change with them—Leo’s successors may have to find another source of unity.

Ghana develops science-based methodology to assess national water stress
items.description: Ghana is taking steps to strengthen its water resource management through a science-based national water stress assessment methodology being developed and piloted with support from the Republic of Korea under UNESCO’s Intergovernmental Hydrological Programme (IHP). The initiative, implemented by UNESCO-IHP in partnership with the World Resources Institute (WRI), seeks to improve understanding of the country’s water resources, identify areas facing increasing water stress and support evidence-based decision-making in response to climate change and other water-related challenges. At a stakeholder validation workshop on the National Water Stress Assessment Methodology for Ghana, representatives from government institutions, research organisations, academia and other stakeholder groups across the water, environment, energy, agriculture and research sectors reviewed the proposed framework, validated data requirements and identified areas for further refinement. Speaking on behalf of the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea to Ghana, Park Kyongsig, the Country Director of the Korea Environmental Industry and Technology Institute (KEITI) in Ghana, Dr Hong Seok Kim, said climate change was placing increasing pressure on water resources through changing rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, droughts and floods. Dr Kim noted that these challenges posed serious threats to water availability, with negative implications for public health, agriculture and economic development. “Water is important not only to human life but also to economic growth and sustainable development,” he said. He reaffirmed Korea’s commitment to supporting Ghana’s water security efforts through international cooperation and technical assistance. Dr Kim stressed that the initiative must go beyond producing technical reports to deliver practical knowledge, strengthen institutions and provide tools that Ghana could continue using beyond the project’s lifespan. According to him, Ghana’s selection as the global pilot country for the development and testing of the methodology demonstrates Korea’s commitment to supporting the country’s sustainable water security agenda. An expert from UNESCO’s Hydrological Systems, Climate Change and Adaptation Sector, Mr Young-Seok Lee, explained that the broader initiative was being implemented in 20 countries across Africa and Asia in two phases. He said the project sought to improve understanding of national water resources by integrating national and international datasets to assess water availability, demand, seasonal variations and pollution challenges. The proposed national assessment methodology is expected to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the country’s water situation and support improved planning and investment in water infrastructure. Technical presentations by World Resources Institute (WRI) experts Zablon Adane and Tinebeb Yohannes focused on Ghana’s water assessment context, existing assessment frameworks, key water management challenges and the need to strengthen the link between scientific data and policy decisions. The Integrated Water Demand Assessment presented at the workshop estimated Ghana’s total water demand at 2,884 cubic metres, covering various sectors, including irrigation, domestic consumption, industrial activities, livestock, environmental needs and hydropower generation. The assessment also put the country’s total annual surface water resources at 36.2 billion cubic metres, while the overall annual water supply volume was estimated at 52.2 billion cubic metres. items.title: Kédougou :La boutique de droit en quête de pérennisation
items.description: Avec 664 dossiers traités depuis juin 2025, la boutique de droit de Kédougou s’impose comme un important outil d’accès à la justice. L’Association des juristes sénégalaises (AJS) plaide pour sa pérennisation, alors que son financement arrive à terme en décembre 2026. La boutique de droit de Kédougou pourrait connaître des difficultés de fonctionnement à partir de décembre 2026, avec la fin du financement de l’Union européenne et de la Fondation Konrad Adenauer. Pour éviter sa fermeture, l’Association des juristes sénégalaises (AJS) a engagé un plaidoyer auprès des autorités, collectivités territoriales et partenaires en vue de trouver un mécanisme de financement durable. Lors d’un panel organisé mercredi à cet effet, Fatou Courou Fall, vice-présidente adjointe chargée des finances de l’AJS, a rappelé que « les besoins des populations n’ont pas de durée déterminée ». Elle préconise également la mise en place d’un comité de suivi associant autorités, populations et médias. Depuis son ouverture, en juin 2025, la structure a traité 664 dossiers, selon sa responsable, Mariame Diarra. Les affaires liées au droit de la famille, notamment l’état civil, les divorces, les répudiations et les violences basées sur le genre, sont les plus fréquentes. Les femmes constituent une part importante des bénéficiaires. La boutique reçoit également des justiciables de Tambacounda. Pour Bintou Diawara, quatrième adjointe au maire de Kédougou, sa disparition priverait de nombreuses personnes, notamment les femmes et les jeunes, d’un précieux service d’écoute et d’orientation juridique. L’enjeu est désormais de mobiliser les acteurs pour préserver cet outil de proximité. Amadou DIOP (Correspondant)

items.title: Avoirs criminels : à Conakry, l’ARINWA veut accélérer la coopération entre États
items.description: Comment retrouver à l’étranger le produit d’un détournement, obtenir sa saisie et préserver sa valeur jusqu’à la décision de justice ? Ces questions sont au cœur de la 13e Assemblée générale annuelle de l’ARINWA, ouverte mercredi 18 novembre 2026 à Conakry sous la présidence du ministre de la Justice et des Droits de l’Homme, Ibrahima Sory II Tounkara. Un annuaire des points focaux tenu à jour, un meilleur suivi des demandes entre pays et des exercices pratiques sur des dossiers de saisie figurent parmi les propositions soumises aux délégations. Le président de l’ARINWA, Mor N’Diaye, a présenté ces pistes à l’ouverture de la rencontre pour rendre plus réactif ce réseau ouest-africain de recouvrement des avoirs, qui compte 16 États membres. Pour 2027, Mor N’Diaye propose de faciliter la prise de contact entre les autorités des différents pays et de suivre chaque demande afin de repérer rapidement les dossiers qui nécessitent l’appui du réseau. Un atelier prévu à Abidjan du 8 au 12 février doit permettre aux participants de travailler sur des cas pratiques, de la localisation d’un bien à l’étranger à la préparation d’une demande de saisie. Le président du réseau souhaite également que les États se dotent d’indicateurs communs pour mesurer les résultats de leur coopération. « Les frontières ne doivent plus constituer des obstacles à l’identification et au recouvrement des avoirs criminels », a déclaré le garde des Sceaux, Ibrahima Sory II Tounkara. Le ministre a mis en avant le rôle de l’Agence de gestion et de recouvrement des avoirs saisis et confisqués (AGRASC) dans l’exécution des décisions de justice et la préservation de la valeur des biens placés sous main de justice. La destination des fonds récupérés figure également au programme des trois jours de travaux. Pour Mohamed Diawara, Directeur général de l’AGRASC et président du comité d’organisation, ces ressources doivent servir à réparer les préjudices et peuvent, conformément aux législations nationales, financer des actions d’intérêt général. « Le crime ne doit jamais constituer une source d’enrichissement », a insisté Mohamed Diawara. Cheick Mouhamad Bamba Niang, représentant régional du projet SecFin Africa, a rappelé que sept des huit États de la sous-région examinés lors du deuxième cycle d’évaluations du GIABA avaient obtenu une faible note pour l’efficacité de leurs dispositifs de confiscation. Citant une estimation de la CNUCED, il a indiqué que les flux financiers illicites coûtaient à l’Afrique près de 88,6 milliards de dollars par an, soit environ 3,7 % de son PIB. Il a plaidé pour des échanges d’informations plus rapides et une meilleure gestion des biens saisis. Safiétou Sy, représentante régionale de l’Office des Nations unies contre la drogue et le crime (ONUDC), a salué le cofinancement de la rencontre par la Guinée. Elle a rappelé que le réseau offre aux enquêteurs, aux procureurs et aux juges un canal informel pour prendre rapidement contact avec leurs homologues. Elle a appelé les États membres à contribuer au fonctionnement de l’ARINWA et à mobiliser leurs points focaux tout au long de l’année, lorsqu’un dossier exige de retrouver ou de saisir un bien au-delà de leurs frontières.

items.title: Cybermenaces et pannes bancaires : Pourquoi le système marocain ne serait pas concerné
items.description: Les récentes pannes informatiques ayant affecté plusieurs grandes banques américaines ne devraient pas avoir de répercussions sur le secteur bancaire marocain. C’est ce qu’affirme une source bien informée du milieu bancaire national, qui attribue ces incidents à des dysfonctionnements strictement locaux, sans lien avec les infrastructures financières du Royaume. S’exprimant auprès de Hespress sous couvert d’anonymat, cette source précise que les perturbations enregistrées au cours des deux derniers jours se sont limitées aux transactions effectuées sur les plateformes et applications numériques propres aux établissements concernés, ainsi qu’à leurs clients établis aux Etats-Unis. Aucun lien technique ni aucune interconnexion avec le système bancaire marocain n’a été relevé, assure-t-elle, excluant toute incidence sur les banques nationales. Parmi les établissements touchés figure JPMorgan Chase , première banque américaine par le volume de ses actifs. Selon plusieurs agences de presse internationales et médias, ses services ont connu des perturbations au cours des deux derniers jours. Un porte-parole de la banque a expliqué que l’incident était dû à « un dysfonctionnement logiciel au niveau des systèmes informatiques internes », tout en écartant l’hypothèse d’une cyberattaque, faute d’éléments permettant de l’étayer. L’établissement a également insisté sur le caractère non systémique de la panne, qui ne concerne pas l’ensemble du secteur bancaire. Il a ensuite annoncé le rétablissement des systèmes et le retour des transactions à la normale. Les transferts internationaux et les opérations financières réglées en devises ne seraient pas davantage concernés. Ces transactions, y compris celles effectuées par les Marocains résidant à l’étranger (MRE), s’appuient sur le réseau SWIFT, présenté par la source comme un système mondial unifié et indépendant, qui ne dépend d’aucune banque en particulier. Leur continuité reste ainsi assurée dans des conditions normales, affirme-t-elle. Un seul scénario pourrait néanmoins entraîner un retard ponctuel : celui d’un transfert envoyé directement depuis le compte d’un client auprès de l’une des banques américaines touchées vers un bénéficiaire se trouvant au Maroc. En dehors de cette éventualité, les clients des établissements bancaires marocains ne devraient subir aucune conséquence, selon la même source. Dans un contexte de multiplication des menaces et des attaques informatiques, la question de la sécurité des transactions bancaires nationales se pose également. Sur ce point, la source écarte tout risque lié aux incidents américains, en soulignant l’absence d’interconnexion entre les systèmes d’exploitation et les applications concernés par les pannes et les infrastructures utilisées au Maroc. Elle rappelle, par ailleurs, que le secteur bancaire national s’appuie sur des développements technologiques internes ainsi que sur des entreprises spécialisées. Ces dispositifs sont accompagnés d’investissements et d’améliorations continus dans les domaines de la cybersécurité et de la protection numérique, destinés à sécuriser l’ensemble des opérations. Sollicité par Hespress, le Groupement professionnel des banques du Maroc (GPBM) n’a toutefois pas pu fournir de déclaration officielle sur le sujet. The post Cybermenaces et pannes bancaires : Pourquoi le système marocain ne serait pas concerné appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: COP 31: African youth urge world leaders to put water at centre of climate adaptation funding
items.description: Young Africans have called on world leaders to prioritise water security in global climate adaptation plans and financing, warning that communities across the continent are already experiencing the effects of climate change through drought, pollution and flooding. The call was made at the ongoing UN climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye, where the African Youth Water and Climate Engagement Initiative presented findings from a continent-wide survey on water and climate challenges. The initiative, led by the Green Africa Youth Organisation (GAYO) with support from the Children’s Investment Fund Foundation (CIFF), surveyed 1,209 young people in 51 African countries and held consultations with 984 others across West, Central, East, North and Southern Africa. The survey found that 76% of respondents felt they had no meaningful say in decisions on water and climate, while only 8% said young people were treated as partners in the decision-making process. It also found that 52% believed their communities were poorly equipped to cope with climate impacts, while 29% said they had lost, or were losing, livelihoods dependent on water. According to the report, young Africans experience climate change largely through its impact on water resources and access. Drought and prolonged water scarcity were identified as the most commonly reported challenges, cited by 44% of respondents. Water pollution followed at 42%, while flooding was reported by 35%. In West Africa, the report highlights coastal erosion and plastic pollution in Ghana and Nigeria, salinisation in Senegal, and drought across the Sahel. The findings also point to the unequal burden of water insecurity, particularly on young people who are responsible for collecting water for their households. One in three respondents said they collected water for their families. Emmanuella Chukwudi, a participant from Nigeria, described the risks girls in her community face when they have to travel to neighbouring villages to find water. “A girl was discovered pregnant after an alleged assault on an occasion she went to fetch water from a neighbouring village. Farmers in my community are also affected,” she said. GAYO’s Climate Director, Baliqees Salaudeen-Ibrahim, said the initiative was designed to understand the continent’s water challenges and document how young people were responding. “What we’re trying to understand is what the current water challenges are on the continent of Africa and how young people are responding to this problem,” she said. She said GAYO would identify youth-led water initiatives with the potential to attract investment, expand their reach and be replicated in other communities. However, the survey identified limited access to funding as a major obstacle to youth-led action. Only 9% of respondents knew of a youth-led initiative that had received funding. Meanwhile, 46% said eligibility requirements excluded them from funding opportunities, while 32% did not know what support was available. The young people are calling for smaller, faster grants ranging from US$500 to US$5,000, alongside mentorship to help develop and expand their initiatives. CIFF Chief Executive Officer Kate Hampton said young people were already implementing solutions in their communities and should be recognised as contributors to climate action. “They have actions that they’re taking in their communities, so we’re trying to show how young people are driving solutions, not just talking about solutions,” she said. Youth take water priorities to global climate negotiations The initiative has outlined 12 youth priorities covering water security, sanitation, climate adaptation finance and water governance. The findings come as African negotiators at COP31 push for an “implementation COP”, with predictable financing for adaptation among the key issues under discussion. The young participants plan to present their evidence at the UN Water Conference in Abu Dhabi from December 8 to 10, before taking their priorities to COP32 in Addis Ababa in 2027. COP31 is scheduled to end on November 20.

items.title: VIDEO: Jeremy Doku names waakye as his favourite Ghanaian food
items.description: Manchester City winger Jeremy Doku has revealed that waakye is his favourite Ghanaian dish, while opening up about his family roots in Kumasi. The Belgium international made the revelation in an interview with Manchester City, where he spoke about his connection to Ghana and his mother’s cooking. “First thing when I think about Ghana is the food. Obviously, I love the food. My mum always cooks for me,” he said. Asked about his favourite dish, Doku said: “We call it waakye. I don’t know how to make it, but my mum knows very well how to make it. It takes a while, takes long. Usually, you have to put a lot of effort in, so I really love it.” The 24-year-old also revealed that he belongs to the Asante ethnic group, adding that both his parents were born in Kumasi.

items.title: Pakistan's mango exports fall 36pc amid US-Iran war: exporters' association
items.description: Pakistan’s mango exports fell 36 per cent this year as the US-Iran war disrupted shipping routes and drove up freight costs, industry figures showed on Wednesday. According to All Pakistan Fruit and Vegetables Exporters Association, the country exported 78,000 tonnes of mangoes this year, compared with 123,000 tons last year. Exports to the Middle East, a major market for Pakistani mangoes, dropped from 36,000 tonnes last year to 14,500 tonnes this year, the association said. Waheed Ahmed, head of the association, told Anadolu that the ongoing conflict had reduced the country’s mango export earnings from approximately $100 million to around $60m. He cited the months-long near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route, and rising freight rates as major factors behind the decline, particularly in exports to Middle Eastern countries. “The freight rate that was $1,000-1,400 before the US-Iran war, now stands at $8,000. Secondly, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz also increased the shipping period , which affected the exports of perishable items like mangoes,” he said. Ahmed said the United Arab Emirates and Oman were the main Middle Eastern destinations for Pakistani mangoes, particularly the internationally acclaimed Chaunsa variety, followed by Saudi Arabia. Kuwait and Qatar also import significant quantities of Pakistani mangoes, according to the association. Mango exports to neighboring Afghanistan were also disrupted by frequent border closures amid strained relations between the two countries, Ahmed said. Pakistan produced 1.9m metric tonnes of mangoes annually until 2018, ranking sixth globally behind India, China, Thailand, Indonesia and Mexico. However, production has declined over the past four years, with the association attributing the drop to global warming. Climate change has reduced Pakistan’s total mango production by 35pc, according to the association.
